title: Man, 30, dies after police use Taser
subtitle: A special investigation team in Alberta has been called in for a second time in a week following the death of a man taken to hospital in critical condition after police tried to subdue him with a Taser.
article: A special investigation team in Alberta has been called in for a second time in a week following the death of a man taken to hospital in critical condition after police tried to subdue him with a Taser.

Gordon Walker Bowe, 30, from Castlegar, B.C., died in Calgary hospital after police used a Taser to try to arrest him Saturday, said Clifton Purvis, executive director of the Alberta serious incident response team.

The independent team, which reviews deaths or serious injuries involving police forces, is also investigating the death of Trevor Grimolfson, who died last Wednesday after Edmonton police used stun guns on him as he was smashing up a pawnshop.
In the Calgary case, police responded to calls of a suspicious person and arrived to find a break-and-enter taking place, Purvis said yesterday.

Officers followed a suspect into the basement of an empty home, where he became combative. Neighbours said it sounded like the man was trying to get away from police. "Subsequent to the deployment, the individual was still combative, police officers had to restrain him physically in an attempt to apprehend him," said Purvis.
Once Bowe was restrained, police arrested and handcuffed him.
He then went into medical distress while being examined by paramedics and was rushed to hospital, where he died the next day.
Purvis said it's unclear whether the Taser deployed successfully or if it even made contact with Bowe.
It will take an autopsy, and examination of the weapon, to figure out what happened, he added.

John Butt, a Vancouver-based consultant in forensic pathology, said it's generally held that because a Taser uses an electric current, if death "doesn't occur instantly, then it's not related to the Taser."
More than 20 people have died in Canada after being stunned by Tasers, but the U.S. company that makes the devices points out they have never been directly blamed for a death.
The company cites independent research that has verified the safety of the devices.
